column13: And it is known that Daat is that which completes the ten sefirot internally, while Keter completes them in their transcendent exteriority. And this is the mystical secret (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13): “Moses from within, Jacob from without.” For Moses our teacher, peace be upon him— embodies the inner secret of Daat; and Jacob in this context, signifies his identity as the primordial root of Israel termed “first” (Reishit); and thus Jacob encompasses all of Israel.

column13: This is “Moses inwardly, Jacob outwardly” (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 13). The outward aspect is the attribute of “truth to Jacob”: everything revealed in him is “a truthful lip established forever.” “Jacob was a wholehearted man,” and wholeheartedness is the opposite of self-devised cleverness. That is, he has no wisdom from himself at all, since he recognizes that everything comes from the blessed God.
column15: “Nor seeking your own pleasure, nor speaking a word”—meaning that even permissible speech, such as praying for one's physical needs, is forbidden on Shabbat when asking explicitly for mundane requirements.

column11: Tikkunei Zohar 85a:3-85b:2: “In Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 48, 85a), the double mention of Shabbat in the verse refers to the union of the Supernal Shabbat (Binah, the World to Come) and the Lower Shabbat (Malkhut, the Sabbath Queen), which illuminate Israel throughout all their dwellings.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 1, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 85a:3-85b:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“And on Shabbat, even in this era, the Blessed Name dwells within the heart of the children of Israel, – as written (Tikun 48): "'Throughout their generations' — fortunate is he who makes for Them...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Yevamot 62a: ‘Rav said: Everyone agrees with regard to a Canaanite slave, that he does not have lineage, as it is written that Abraham said to his slaves: “Remain here with the donkey” (Genesis 22:5). column11: Sotah 21a: ‘The Gemara asks: Does the merit of a mitzva protect one so much as to delay her punishment? But isn’t it taught in a baraita: Rabbi Menaḥem bar Yosei interpreted this verse homiletically: “For the mitzva is a lamp and the Torah is light” (Proverbs 6:23). The verse associates the mitzva with a lamp and the Torah with the light of the sun. The mitzva is associated with a lamp in order to say to you: Just as a lamp does not protect one by its light extensively but only temporarily, while the lamp is in one’s hand, so too, a mitzva protects one only temporarily, i.e., while one is performing the mitzva.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 21a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as we explained regarding what is stated in the Gemara (Sotah 21a): "Scripture hung the commandment upon a lamp and the Torah upon light, etc., to tell you: just as a lamp shines only temporarily,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 14:31: “‘And Israel saw the great work which the Lord did upon the Egyptians, and the people feared the Lord; and they believed in the Lord, and in His servant Moses’ (Exodus 14:31): Great is faith (emunah) before Him who spoke and the world came into being, for in the merit of the faith wherewith Israel believed in the Lord, the Holy Spirit (Ruach HaKodesh) rested upon them and they uttered the Song at the Sea.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 14:31) to illuminate his exposition here (“And behold it is found in the Mechilta and Midrash Rabbah (Beshalach): "And in the merit of faith the Holy Spirit rested upon them and they uttered song, as it is said: 'And they believed, etc.,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: That even those submerged in the deepest immersion in the mundane affairs of this world possess an inner root cleaved unto the Blessed Name; and this is the root of faith, they being "believers, the children of believers" (Shabbat 97a); and immediately when Moshe Rabbeinu came and aroused them, "and the people believed" (Shemos 4:31) immediately in the Blessed Name; and in the merit of faith they were redeemed (Mechilta, Beshalach 6); meaning that through this the light awakened little by little within their hearts, until they merited to emerge from darkness into great light.

column15: Yet our father Avraham found no satisfaction even in such delight, and even in wealth capable of lasting many thousands of years, because he knew that all this is merely temporary life bound by borders, and why should he delight in that?! Behold it is in Hashem's great power to bequeath eternal life without any limit!

column11: Mekhilta d'Rabbi Yishmael 15:2: “‘This is my God, and I will glorify Him’ (Exodus 15:2): Rabbi Eliezer says, Whence do you say that a maidservant saw at the Red Sea what Isaiah and Ezekiel and all the other prophets never saw? column13: Such a person merits complete redemption from all the illusions of this world, becoming liberated from the yetzer hara; and this is the redemption from Egypt which occurred in Nissan, when they emerged suddenly from the grip of imagination and the immense immersion wherein they lay in absolute darkness into a great light, until a simple handmaid at the Sea witnessed visions greater than the prophet Yechezkel (Mechilta, Beshalach 3); and likewise in Nissan they are destined to be redeemed in the ultimate Future (Rosh Hashanah 11a).
column15: And as ruled by the Rosh (Bava Metzia, ch. 2): In an incident where one bought silver thinking it was tin, and the seller was unaware it was silver, Rabbi Eliezer of Metz ruled the buyer acquired it, because the seller lacked knowledge that it was silver when purchasing it from a non-Jew —.

column11: Zohar, Beshalach 54a: “In the Zohar (Beshalach II 54a), the word ‘Then [sang Moses]’ is expounded as the union of Aleph (1, the primordial wonder of Atika / Keter) radiating into Zayin (7, the seven lower Sefirot culminating in Malkhut)—producing the supernal light of Eight (Chet / Chanukah and circumcision).” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Beshalach 54a) to illuminate his exposition here (“according to what is written in the Holy Zohar (ibid. 54a): "When the light of the Ancient One shines, etc., the radiance of the aleph reaches the zayin, etc." And this means that aleph points to...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Which represents the acute dialectic of Torah given as a gift to Moses, who acted generously and transmitted it to Israel [ibid.]; and dialectic is the give-and-take of the Oral Torah, which cannot be attained except through debate in halakhah, standing upon authentic truth through analysis.
column15: As taught in the Holy Zohar (Beshalach 44a): It is the customary way of the world that when a person rises from his bed, the sheet he slept upon emits an unrefined, repulsive odor; but when Elisha arose, the sheet emitted a fragrance like the Garden of Eden.

column11: Zohar, Terumah 137b: “In the Zohar (Terumah II 137b, variant reading), the distinction in Deuteronomy 31:9 (‘And Moses wrote this Torah, and delivered it unto the priests the sons of Levi’) is noted: the Written Torah scroll was handed over to the custody of the priests and Levites, whereas the transmission of the Oral Torah was delivered to Joshua (`Moses received the Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua`).” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Terumah 137b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and it is based on what is written in the Holy Zohar (ibid. 137b in other editions) on the teaching: "Moses received Torah from Sinai and transmitted it to Joshua", and they applied it to the Oral...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And as I wrote elsewhere regarding the two Messiahs, ben David and ben Yosef, who correspond to "I am" and "You shall not have," Rabbi Akiva corresponding to "You shall not have" as written above (folio 36a)], a scholar can be his bar mazaleih in some particular dimension, since Akiva is a primary soul-root [from the aspect of "You shall not have," encompassing all negative commandments], yet this is only a partial connection; but regarding a "Halachah to Moses from Sinai," this is not termed the personal words of Moses so as to say one must share his soul-root, for Moses received it directly from Sinai, namely from Hashem, blessed be He.
column15: As in the Zohar (Behar 111b): In two manners are Israel designated before the Holy One: they are called servants, as written: “for they are My servants”; and they are called children, as written: “You are the children of the Lord your God”.

column11: Nedarim 22b: ‘Rav Adda, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: Had Israel not sinned in earlier times they would have been given the five books of the Torah and the book of Joshua alone. They needed the book of Joshua because it includes the arrangement of Eretz Yisrael. Since it contains the division of Eretz Yisrael among the tribes, it was required for all generations, but the other books of the prophets primarily detail the history of how Israel angered God and He sent prophets to admonish them. What is the reason, i.e., what is the allusion to this idea? It is stated: “For in much wisdom is much vexation” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). column12: Likkutei Maamarim, On Book of Joshua:17
column13: Therefore the Book of Joshua is the allocation of the Land of Israel (Nedarim 22b); a "book" being the inscription of wisdom as noted above, meaning the engraving of his soul-faculty, and his soul-faculty was the division and allotment of the Land of Israel, not the physical terrain itself, but its allotment, settlement, and assignment to the tribes.
column15: And the reason was that Noah contented himself with what was promised to him personally—that he himself would be among the inheritors of the World to Come—and did not exert himself to pray for his descendants after him, that an enduring remnant for eternal life should survive from him throughout future generations.

column11: Zohar, Pinchas 85:572-87:582: “In the Zohar (Pinchas III 243a), the verse ‘Because of this our heart is faint (davah libeinu)’ (Lamentations 5:17) and ‘Make me to hear joy and gladness’ (Psalms 51:10) are expounded upon the attribute of Hod (the fifth of the lower Sefirot, corresponding to the fifth millennium and the left pillar of the limbs), which languishes in exile until illuminated by the miracle of Chanukah and the Oral Torah.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Pinchas 85:572-87:582) to illuminate his exposition here (“And this is the meaning of what is written in the Holy Zohar (Part III, 243a): – "'All day faint' — this is Hod, from the side of Hod, the fifth millennium the Holy Temple remained desolate". column13: And then they remove from him the burdensome yoke of worldly labor (Avos 3:5), meriting bread from heaven as occurred in concrete reality in the generation of the wilderness. And that miracle impressed its prototype for all future generations, as written in the Yalkut: that the pillar of Manna was two thousand cubits high; and it appears to me that this alludes to the two thousand years of Torah (Avodah Zarah 9a), all those generations being nourished from its spiritual energy.
column15: And concerning this it is said (Psalms 104:15): “And wine gladdens the heart of man,” for from this stems that giddy joy, because it conceals and confounds the mind until he fails to perceive an Overseer in the world.

column11: Avodah Zarah 9a: ‘In relation to the discussion on the calculation of years, the Gemara states that one of the Sages of the school of Eliyahu taught: The world is destined to exist for six thousand years. For two thousand years the world was waste, as the Torah had not yet been given. The next set of two thousand years are the time period of the Torah. The last set of two thousand years are the period designated for the days of the Messiah, but due to our many sins there are those years that have been taken from them, i.e., such and such years have already passed and have been taken from the two thousand years that are designated for the Messiah, and the Messiah has not yet arrived. column13: Now the count of 2448 years until the Exodus from Egypt is detailed in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (9a), see there in Rashi that we calculate the years of each generation lived before his son, for subsequent years are assigned to the son, and you reckon from Adam the First, etc., examine the calculation there and see that it counts from the birth of Adam, since the chronology is derived directly from the lifespan of Adam.
column15: While to the sons of Noah was given enduring existence across the span of the six thousand years, having been trained in derech eretz through the ruin of the early generations, no longer to expand into worldly pleasure beyond proper limits.

column11: Zohar, Vayera 29:438-30:444: “In the Zohar (Vayera I 116b–117a), the six millennia of world history are aligned with the six days of Creation and the six Sefirot from Chesed to Yesod: the fifth millennium corresponds to Hod (concerning which it is said ‘all the day faint,’ Lamentations 1:13), a time of deep exile illuminated by the Chanukah lights, whereas in the sixth millennium (Yesod) the gates of wisdom open in preparation for the cosmic Shabbat.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vayera 29:438-30:444) to illuminate his exposition here (“However in the fifth millennium "all day faint", as written in the Holy Zohar (Part I, 116b), and it was the commandment of the elders to kindle Chanukah lights to make a dedication for the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Experiencing vibrant life then even when the opposing reality of death has ceased. And as I heard on the Tikkunim: "You are wise without known wisdom, understanding without known understanding"— Chochmah being intellectual cognition in the brain and Binah being the feeling of the heart; angels possessing intellectual knowledge channeled by Hashem without the emotional heartbeat [for heart-perception is impossible without the counter-presence of an opposing force.

column15: And this corresponds to the mystery of Ehyeh, for this Name indicates that the time has not yet arrived for the good to be fully given into man's hand; only after time elapses will the Holy One draw the good out from its sheath, and the Name Havayah will manifest in wholeness and be delivered into human grasp, for upon actual reception the Name Havayah rests upon the entity.

column11: Berakhot 33a: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan replied that that would be impossible, as the customs associated with havdala went through several stages. He said to him: Initially, during the difficult, early years of the Second Temple, they established that havdala is to be recited in the Amida prayer. Subsequently, when the people became wealthy, they established that havdala is to be recited over the cup of wine. When the people became impoverished, they again established that it was to be recited in the Amida prayer. column13: "And the Tree of Knowledge"—this is the brain, which distinguishes between good and evil, as written in Berakhot 33a: "If there is no knowledge, whence is separation?". And the subdivision of these four powers— constitutes the perfection of the human form: brain, heart, and the vessels of action which divide into two: the concrete act itself is "pleasant to the sight", and its internal spiritual purpose is "good for food" and they are two trees: a tree pleasant to sight and a tree good for food, as I heard.

column11: Pesachim 87b: ‘Rabbi Oshaya said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “The righteous acts of His rulers [pirzono] in Israel” (Judges 5:11)? The Holy One, Blessed be He, performed a charitable deed toward Israel in that He scattered them [pizran] among the nations; had He exiled them to one place, they could have all been destroyed at once. And this concept is that which a certain apostate said to Rabbi Ḥanina: We gentiles are superior to you Jews in that we have patience. It is written of you: “For Joab and all Israel remained there six months until he had cut off every male in Edom” (I Kings 11:16), whereas we, although you have been with us for several years, are not doing anything to you.…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 87b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and it is based on what is written in the holy books on the statement (Pesachim 87b): "The Holy One exiled Israel solely so that converts would be added to them", where the meaning is not that...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And in Pesachim [87b] they taught that Israel was exiled to Babylonia so they would eat dates and engage in Torah, referring to the Oral Torah established in Babylonia; as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that honey accustoms the tongue to Torah, which is why dates are termed "honey" in the Torah; and Malkhut, which is the mouth, is designated the Oral Torah (Tikkunei Zohar 17a).

column15: For in every individual detail there exists an intermingling of darkness and light, and how could the darkness of this person unite with the light of his fellow so that they all form a single band?! It proves that all this is because Hashem, Who is One and perfect in all wholeness, dwells among them, and through this they too are able to unite.

column11: Berakhot 9b: ‘Having explained the use of the double language of “I will be that I will be,” the Gemara proceeds to explain the double language employed by Elijah on Mount Carmel: “Answer me, Lord, answer me, that this people will know that You are the Lord, God, and You have turned their hearts backward” (I Kings 18:37). Rabbi Abbahu said: Why did Elijah say answer me twice? This repetition teaches that Elijah said before the Holy One, Blessed be He: Master of the Universe, answer me that fire will descend from heaven and consume everything that is on the altar, and answer me that You will divert their mind from devising alternative explanations for what they witnessed so that they will not say that…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 9b) to illuminate his exposition here (“which they explained (Berachot 9b): "They made it like a trap without grain, like the depths of the sea without fish". And this means "fish" points to the pristine root of life, for regarding fish...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And regarding this they alluded: "Greater was the plunder at the Sea than the plunder in Egypt, etc." (Berachos 9b); for Egypt they rendered "like a seabed without fish" (Berachos 9b), which alludes to the harvesting and extraction of all the holy sparks that were embedded there; and this occurred by way of the spoils of war, even though the Egyptians lent them of their own accord; while what remained in Israel's hands subsequently was perforce plunder, for the Egyptians had given it merely as a temporary loan.

column15: Wherefore he clamored and marveled: "Can one say that the world is without a governor?!" and Hashem said to him: "I am the Master of the universe." And that is: in truth Hashem directs the entire universe, and nothing is enacted apart from Him, blessed be He, and what man does is encompassed in Hashem's will; yet through whom does Hashem execute His emissary-mission to fulfill His will?

column11: Zohar, Bo 4:80-92: ‘R. Hezekiah drew the same inference from the verse, “And the Lord shall smite Egypt, smiting and healing” (Isa. 19, 22), i.e. smiting the Egyptians and healing Israel, to wit, from the wound of circumcision,’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Bo 4:80-92) to illuminate his exposition here (“(after the manner expounded in Zohar Part II, 36a), in that through each plague Israel emerged from one trait among the ten traits in the kelipah "parallel one to another", and entered into the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For the blood is the life-soul; and when a person offers his very soul to the Blessed Name, this manifests as judgment to Egypt and mercy to Israel, as it is written in the Zohar (Bo 36a), for concerning "upon the entrance" the Zohar explains there: the entrance of the body is circumcision, which is the inception of bodily construction and the birth of the Jewish person, to be dedicated to the Blessed Name from birth, from the womb.
column15: And then he was promised (ibid., vv. 11–15): “Moreover the Lord tells you that the Lord will make you a house: when your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever... but My mercy shall not depart from him.”

column13: And on every Purim we merit this transcendent illumination, which is an inkling of Shabbat which is an inkling of the World to Come, where the effort of 'Israel sanctifies the seasons' does not operate, rather an inherent, fixed, and enduring holiness. And likewise Purim does not depend upon the conscious sanctification of Israel, for its central mitzvah is observed through intoxication 'until he knows not', leaving no room for calculated striving; rather that day was chosen through the lot on its own.
column15: For concerning the earth it is written (Isaiah 6:3): “The whole earth is full of His glory,” and concerning heaven it is written (Psalms 113:4): “His glory is above the heavens,” but concerning the sea no explicit revelation of glory is mentioned.

column11: Yoma 72b: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, as he has no heart?” (Proverbs 17:16)? This expresses the following sentiment: Woe to them, haters of Torah scholars, a euphemism for the Torah scholars themselves, who immerse themselves in Torah and have no fear of Heaven. They are fools; they try to acquire the wisdom of Torah, but since they have no fear of Heaven in their hearts they lack the ability to do so.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and regarding one who engages in Torah without fear of Heaven they said (Yoma 72b): – "'Why is there a price in the hand of a fool, etc.' — they engage in Torah but possess no fear of Heaven...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And in Yoma (72b): "'The fear of Hashem is pure, enduring forever'—this refers to one who studies Torah in purity. What is this? He marries a wife and studies Torah thereafter": the meaning is that Torah drawn from reverent awe is a Torah of purity, for anything influenced by animalistic bodily self-interest is termed "impurity."
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:10
column15: And this is the meaning of 'the master of the palace gazed upon him'— namely that Hashem, blessed be He, concurred upon this truth, that in such unity Hashem delights, and it is titled 'an assembly for the sake of Heaven.' For if the root of their intent is not for the sake of Heaven, then what does their union and collective association avail them?!

column11: Zohar, Beshalach 13:178-14:190: ‘Said R. column13: At night it is the Apple Field (Chakal Tapuchin)—yearning, the feminine attribute; by day it is Atika Kadisha, the level of Ayin, beyond desire (Zohar Beshalach 52b on "Why do you cry to Me? It depends on Atika"), influencing the root of the soul above intellect and conscious desire. At the third meal as Shabbat departs, Ze'ir Anpin fulfills the desire, channeling the influx for the entire coming week.

column11: Pesachim 118a: ‘Rav Ḥisda said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Give thanks to the Lord for He is good” (Psalms 136:1)? Scripture informs us: The Lord will give strength unto His…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3) to illuminate his exposition here (“"The people walking in darkness have seen a great light" is applied (in Tanchuma Noach 3) to the Oral Torah; – and so they said (Megillah 16b): "'To the Jews was light' — this is Torah", for this...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this constitutes a wealth of greater wisdom, the deep intellect of sharpening halakhah emerging through this, and the Holy One rejoices in dialectical study; and this issues from concealment wherein light is not revealed, as the Sages expounded in Tanchuma [Noach 3] on "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light" [Isaiah 9:1] regarding the Oral Torah; and in Sanhedrin (24a) on "He has set me in dark places" [Lamentations 3:6]—this is the Babylonian Talmud, where the depth of analytical debate was revealed.
column15: So it is with Klal Yisrael as a whole, and so with every individual: prior to the revelation of his unique portion in Torah, he traverses the stages of darkness and tohu, followed by the five ascending gradations of light, as elucidated above.

column11: Megillah 16b: ‘§ The Gemara returns to its explanation of the Megilla. The verse states: “The Jews had light and gladness, and joy and honor” (Esther 8:16). Rav Yehuda said: “Light”; this is referring to the Torah that they once again studied. And similarly it says: “For the mitzva is a lamp and the Torah is light” (Proverbs 6:23). “Gladness” [simḥa]; this is referring to the Festivals that they once again observed. And similarly it says: “And you shall be glad [vesamakhta] on your Festival” (Deuteronomy 16:14). “Joy” [sasson]; this is referring to circumcision, as they once again circumcised their sons. And similarly it says: “I rejoice [sas] at Your word” (Psalms 119:162), which the Sages understood…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 16b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and so they said (Megillah 16b): "'To the Jews was light' — this is Torah", for this is the underlying goal of the entire Torah, the 613 commandments being 613 counsels (Zohar Part II, 82b),...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: While contemplation and holy joy generate alacrity and spiritual awakening; and "Gladness" (Sasson) and "Honor" (Yakar) are the holy thoughts that subsequently enter, drawn from Light and Joy; and to channel into all faculties of action and concrete deeds themselves holiness and pure intention for the sake of Heaven in all things.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 7:2
column15: And that is: when Avraham our Father saw that the sun rose and set, and the moon shed its light, and in the morning the sun shone again while the moon's light faded, he then understood that there exists an Exalted One above them Who governs all; for that which is truly great is not pushed aside by that which is smaller, whereas these celestial bodies displace one another.

column11: Zohar, Yitro 19:324-20:333: ‘We have been taught that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave six hundred and thirteen counsels unto man, in order that he might be perfect in attachment to his Lord, for the Holy King desires only his good, both in this world and in the world to come; but more especially in the world to come, since whatever good the Holy One bestows upon man in this world is taken from the sum of good which he is entitled to receive in the world to come. Why is this? Because, as we have been taught, the world to come is, as it were, God’s own possession. This is not to say, of course, that this present world is not His also,’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Yitro 19:324-20:333) to illuminate his exposition here (“the 613 commandments being 613 counsels (Zohar Part II, 82b), meaning pathways to illuminate His divine light within the human heart; and therefore they said regarding the future: "And they shall...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: 2 (§4): And the Blessed Name provides counsel for all, the 613 commandments being 613 divine strategies (eitin, Zohar II, 82b) how to attain the truth and cleave unto the Living God; even after the estrangement caused by the sin of Adam, subsequent generations, and one's personal transgressions; with all this the Blessed Name orchestrates remedies so that no outcast of Israel be expelled from Him (II Shmuel 14:14); and toward this operate the six festival days of the year: the first and seventh days of Pesach, Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, the first day of Succos, and Shemini Atzeret.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 47:2
column15: And that is: because His light is impossible for any creature to receive; yet the order of this world dictates that Hashem bestow His light in gradation according to what creatures are capable of bearing, since creatures contract themselves in order to receive His light; and all this is for the benefit of creatures, for from His perspective He has no need for this.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 2: ‘Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon interpreted the verses regarding the generations. “The earth was emptiness and disorder” – this is Adam the first man, who became oblivion and nothingness. “And disorder” – this is Cain, who sought to restore the world to emptiness and disorder. “And darkness” – this is the generation of Enosh, 23:7). based on the verse: “Their actions are in the dark and they say: Who sees us and who knows of us?” (Isaiah 29:15). “Upon the face of the depths” – this is the generation of the Flood, as it is stated: “On that day all the wellsprings of the great depths were breached” (Genesis 7:11). “And the spirit [ruaḥ] of God was hovering over the surface of the water” – based on…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 2) to illuminate his exposition here (“and regarding this they said (Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 2): "The Holy One, Blessed be He, said: How long will the world proceed in darkness; let the light arrive; – and some say: 'Let there be...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: That is: the first day is the beginning of Creation, establishing the foundations of created existence. As Rabbeinu Moshe ben Nachman explained regarding 'formless and void,' 'spirit,' 'darkness,' 'light,' and 'water'—see his words there and the other commentators— all of these allude to the elemental foundations of created beings and to the beginning of every created thing.
column15: And likewise, concerning the unbridled indulgence characterizing the early generations—the Generation of the Flood, the Generation of the Dispersion, and the men of Sodom—from this angle too it seemed unnecessary for the Torah to begin from Genesis to record this.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 11: ‘“God blessed the seventh day [and sanctified it]” – Rabbi Yishmael said: He blessed it with manna and He sanctified it with manna. He blessed it with manna in that all the days of the week one omer [of manna] would fall, while on the day before Shabbat two omers would fall. for Shabbat. He sanctified it with manna, as it did not fall on it [on Shabbat] at all. Rabbi Natan says: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it with a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak said: He blessed it with manna and sanctified it through the gatherer. He blessed it with apparel. Rav Huna said: He should change his clothing. Rabbi Ḥiyya said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: He should mix [garments]. Avin bar Ḥisdai said:…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 11) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as written (in Bereishit Rabbah, Parashah 11) that the Holy One provided him two flints and he struck them against one another and light emerged from them, and he recited over it the blessing...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: From this arises the first recognition available to created beings: that there is a Creator, as Abraham our father, peace be upon him, recognized through the principle that a palace cannot exist without a master. It is stated at the end of Sefer Yetzirah that all of his wisdom lay in the combinations of the letters through which heaven and earth were created.
column15: And the name Chavah with a Vav is as taught by the Ari in Likutei Torah (Parashat Bereishit), that the spelled-out letters of the Name Havayah numerically equal Chavah (19), whereas simply she should have been named Chayah.

column11: Pesachim 2b: ‘The Gemara raises an objection: “And I say, yet the darkness shall envelop me, and the or about me shall be night” (Psalms 139:11). Apparently, or is day. The Gemara rejects this proof. This is what David is saying there: I said after I sinned that darkness shall envelop me in the World-to-Come, which is like day. Now that I know that I have been forgiven, even this world, which is like darkness, is light for me. That being the case, it cannot be derived from here that the word or describes the day.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 2b) to illuminate his exposition here (“to illuminate the darkness of the night of this world which resembles night, as written (Pesachim 2b): for behold physical luminaries created by the Blessed Name are two: the light of the sun and...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And perhaps this is the meaning of the statement of the Zohar (III, 161a) at the end of Parashat Shelach: that the Shechinah never departs from Israel, even on secular workdays; for this is the entire sanctity of Shabbat the Queen, the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and the resting of His Shechinah who conceals Herself with us in exile and in this world which is likened unto night; but in the World to Come which is likened unto day, as stated at the beginning of Pesachim (2b): "yet shall not your Teacher be hidden any more" (Yeshayah 30:20), there being no further concealment.
column15: To understand how the concept of darkness could apply before the creation of the world, when concerning the Blessed Name it is written (Psalms 139:12): “Even darkness obscures not from You, and night shines like the day, etc.”

column11: Nedarim 22b: ‘Rav Adda, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said: Had Israel not sinned in earlier times they would have been given the five books of the Torah and the book of Joshua alone. They needed the book of Joshua because it includes the arrangement of Eretz Yisrael. Since it contains the division of Eretz Yisrael among the tribes, it was required for all generations, but the other books of the prophets primarily detail the history of how Israel angered God and He sent prophets to admonish them. What is the reason, i.e., what is the allusion to this idea? It is stated: “For in much wisdom is much vexation” (Ecclesiastes 1:18). All the wisdom that the Jews possess from the books of the Bible is the result of…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Nedarim 22b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and "had Israel not sinned they would have been given only the Five Books of the Torah, etc." (Nedarim 22b); and on this it is said: "For in much wisdom is much grief". And at the giving of the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And had Israel not sinned, they would have been given only the Pentateuch and the Book of Joshua alone, as written in Nedarim (22b). And all the rest of the Prophets and Writings, and certainly the Oral Torah, emerged on account of human shortcomings; through abundant vexation, they required abundant wisdom. And through these shortcomings, the strict judgment sometimes dictates that substitutions occur, God forbid, among Israelites themselves.
column15: For since He commanded “Let there be light,” why say “and there was light” when “and it was so” would suffice? Because five distinct rungs branched and flowed from this primordial light (see there, and above section 34).

column11: Avodah Zarah 5a: ‘The Gemara answers: Do not say that if our ancestors had not sinned we would not have come into the world, as we still would have been born; rather, it would have been as though we had not come into the world. We would have been of no importance, due to the previous generations that would have still been alive. The Gemara asks: Is this to say that if the Jewish people had not sinned with the Golden Calf then they would not have died? But isn’t the chapter that addresses widows whose husbands die childless (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) written in the Torah, and the chapter that addresses the inheritance a deceased father bequeaths to his sons (Numbers 27:8–11) is also written?’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 5a) to illuminate his exposition here (“meaning as written (Avodah Zarah 5a) that there was freedom from the Angel of Death, for they would not die, and the Angel of Death is identical with the Evil Inclination; and they were on the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: 5 (§4): Which is the perception of absolute union, for "man shall not see Me and live" (Shemos 33:20); experienced solely at Sinai before the Golden Calf; concerning which it was said: "Did ever people hear the voice of God... as you have heard, and live?" (Devarim 4:33); being then on the rung of: "I said: You are godlike beings, and all of you sons of the Most High" (Tehillim 82:6); liberated from the yetzer hara and the Angel of Death (Avodah Zarah 5a); and these are the two crowns corresponding to Na'aseh and Nishma.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 46:7
column15: And the reason Avraham our Father did not circumcise himself prior to this, inasmuch as he fulfilled the entire Torah: for the halakhah in the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 27a) is: that one who is circumcised may circumcise, while one uncircumcised may not circumcise; wherefore so long as Hashem's utterance was not spoken to him “As for Me, behold, My covenant is with you”, he was not yet legally termed 'circumcised', and consequently could not perform circumcision upon himself.

column11: Eruvin 13b: ‘As in the mishna that we learned: In the case of one whose head and most of his body were in the sukka, but his table was in the house, Beit Shammai deem this sukka invalid; and Beit Hillel deem it valid. Beit Hillel said to Beit Shammai: Wasn’t there an incident in which the Elders of Beit Shammai and the Elders of Beit Hillel went to visit Rabbi Yoḥanan ben HaḤoranit, and they found him sitting with his head and most of his body in the sukka, but his table was in the house? Beit Shammai said to them: From there do you seek to adduce a proof? Those visitors, too, said to him: If that was the manner in which you were accustomed to perform the mitzva, you have never fulfilled the mitzva…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 13b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And as they said (Eruvin 13b): "These and those are the words of the Living God", and (Chagigah 3b): "All were given from one Shepherd, from the mouth of the Master of all works"; – and likewise...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: 2: This resulted from the breaking of the first Tablets, which caused man to learn Torah and forget it (Eruvin 54a); for had they remained worthy, all would have been visibly explicit in the Written Torah without needing oral deductions, rendering forgetfulness impossible; but following the sin, the luminous clarity of the first Tablets was concealed within the second Tablets, making revelation accessible only through obscurity; yet despite the lack of uniform consensus, "both these and those are the words of the living God," all part of Torah.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:2
column15: And the meaning in this is as brought in Mei HaShiloach: "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself"— meaning, if you arrived at novel Torah insights, 'you are wise for yourself', for all novelty is solely from your perspective, yet to the Torah itself you added no novelty whatsoever, because in truth this too was encompassed in the Torah only that from you it had been concealed until now.

column11: Chagigah 3b: ‘This difference is important, because the first consecration of Eretz Yisrael, by those who ascended from Egypt, caused it to be sanctified only for its time and it was not sanctified forever, as that depended on the renewed conquest of the land by the Jewish people. And those who ascended from Babylonia left those cities aside and did not consider them part of Eretz Yisrael even after Jewish settlement was renewed there. They would plow and harvest in these places in the Sabbatical Year and tithe the poor man’s tithe, so that the poor of Eretz Yisrael, who did not have sufficient income from the previous years, could rely upon that produce in the Sabbatical Year, receiving help from…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 3b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and (Chagigah 3b): "All were given from one Shepherd, from the mouth of the Master of all works"; – and likewise (Shabbat 138b): "'To seek the word of Hashem' — this is Halachah, etc., – 'and they...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Scripture stated this regarding seeking and learning Torah from his mouth, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:10): "They shall teach Jacob Your judgments"; and in Yoma (26a): You will not find a seasoned rabbinic scholar who issues authoritative halakhic rulings unless he descends from Levi or Issachar. And this is because in every halakhic judgment there exist uncertainties and balanced considerations to this side and to that side, and the Sages have already affirmed in Eruvin (13b) and Chagigah (3b) that although these forbid and those permit, "both these and those are the words of the living God," and all were given from one Shepherd.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 16:5
column15: And so it is said of them (Numbers 23:22): “He has as it were the strength of a wild-ox (re'em)”: and that is: in the future Hashem will deliver from all of these: “To'afot” points to an impulsive action devoid of conscious intellect, for it derives from swift flight, which corresponds to the land of Canaan; and “Re'em” points to an action executed with mighty power and deliberate fortitude, even though it operates in free choice and composure of mind; and in the future Hashem will redeem all of this, refining everything unto goodness.

column11: Shabbat 138b: ‘The Sages taught a similar idea in the Tosefta: When our Sages entered the vineyard in Yavne, they said: The Torah is destined to be forgotten from the Jewish people, as it is stated: “Behold, days are approaching, says the Lord God, and I will send forth a hunger in the land, not a hunger for bread and not a thirst for water, but for hearing the words of the Lord” (Amos 8:11). And it states: “And they will drift from sea to sea, and from north to east they will roam to find the word of the Lord, but they will not find it” (Amos 8:12).’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 138b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and (Chagigah 3b): "All were given from one Shepherd, from the mouth of the Master of all works"; – and likewise (Shabbat 138b): "'To seek the word of Hashem' — this is Halachah, etc., – 'and they...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: This is the mystery of the Torah deriving from the foundation of the Father (Yesod d'Abba), whose illumination penetrates the feminine receptacle (Nukva) and shines through the hearts of Israel's sages; fulfilling the divine promise: "For it shall not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed." And in Shabbat [138b] they said: in the future the Torah is destined to be forgotten, meaning there will be no unambiguous halakhic consensus; for absolute clarity was the hallmark of the Written Torah, whereas the Oral Torah is characterized by disputing voices—some forbidding, others permitting—the ultimate word of Hashem remaining veiled.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:18 (§2)
column15: And if an assembly unites and forms a single collective with this pure intention to crown over themselves Hashem Who is One, then within this assembly there will be consummate wholeness without any division; and even if one states a halakhic ruling and his colleague disputes him and rules the opposite, nonetheless they are perfectly harmonious at the root, and there in their words there is no division, since their intention is one, and as brought in the Talmud (Pesachim 53b).

column11: Shabbat 138b: ‘The Sages taught a similar idea in the Tosefta: When our Sages entered the vineyard in Yavne, they said: The Torah is destined to be forgotten from the Jewish people, as it is stated: “Behold, days are approaching, says the Lord God, and I will send forth a hunger in the land, not a hunger for bread and not a thirst for water, but for hearing the words of the Lord” (Amos 8:11). And it states: “And they will drift from sea to sea, and from north to east they will roam to find the word of the Lord, but they will not find it” (Amos 8:12).’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 138b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and likewise (Shabbat 138b): "'To seek the word of Hashem' — this is Halachah, etc., – 'and they shall not find it' — that they will not find a clear Halachah and clear Mishnah in one place",...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Becoming free from the yetzer hara like ministering angels. And though after the Golden Calf the yetzer returned to its place; nevertheless once conquered through Torah, man returns to this power of Na'aseh; and subsequently merits consummate hearing (Nishma): "unto the voice of His word—the word of Hashem is Halachah"; as stated in Shabbat (138b), Sanhedrin (87a), and Keritot (13b); this being the Holy Spirit of the Oral Torah poured into Jewish hearts to perceive halachic truth.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 6:5
column15: And this is likewise why they instituted in the formulation of all blessings to say “Blessed are You”: for from man's perspective, how could it be fitting to address the King of kings in the direct second-person?! Behold Hashem is concealed from the eyes of all living and no likeness is seen of Him! Rather, the divine spark from Above residing in man, that power articulates 'Blessed are You' facing Hashem directly.

column11: Zohar, Vayechi 53:517-528: ‘When Jacob said to his sons, “I will tell you what will befall you in the latter end of days”, a kind of sadness came over him and the Shekinah departed. His sons, however, raised their voices and said, “Hear, O Israel, etc.”, and Jacob answered, “Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom for ever and ever”, and on this proclamation of the unity the Shekinah returned to its place. AND JACOB CALLED. The word ‘called’ signifies that he established them in their place above and below.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vayechi 53:517-528) to illuminate his exposition here (“an utterance in quiet secrecy, as you say "and you said in your heart" (Zohar Part I, 234b); and this is the Oral Torah which the Blessed Name shines into the heart of the Sages; and it resembles...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, who told his sons: "that which shall befall you in the last days" (Bereishis 49:1), utilizing the term mikreh (chance occurrence); meaning regarding all temporal matters of this world which are fleeting like chance accidents, he revealed the inward truth hidden within them; for every "telling" (haggadah) operates in the secret of supernal wisdom (Zohar, Vayechi 234b).
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 33:2
column15: And the concept is: behold Avraham our Father innovated in the world to transform the third-person 'He' (Hu) into the direct second-person 'You' (Attah). And that is: Hashem divided the world into thirds: one-third inhabited land, one-third sea, one-third wilderness. In inhabited civilization dwells the mystery of 'You', where human beings dwell and Hashem bestows upon them all blessings, and creatures offer thanks, praise, and glorify their Maker over His kingdom.

column11: Taanit 9a: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan sat down and wondered aloud about this verse, saying: Is there anything that is written in the Writings that is not alluded to in the Torah at all? I cannot think of any hint of this idea in the Torah itself. The child said to him: Is that to say that this idea is really not alluded to in the Torah? But isn’t it written, with regard to Joseph’s brothers: “And their heart failed them and they turned trembling to one to another, saying: What is this that God has done to us?” (Genesis 42:28). This verse exemplifies the notion that when one sins and encounters troubles, he wonders why it is happening to him.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 9a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as they said (Ta'anit 9a) even regarding passages in the Writings: "There is nothing that is not alluded to in the Torah"; and on this they said (Eruvin 21b) on the verse "His locks are curled":...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column15: Just as a son is initially enfolded in potentia within his father, and upon emerging into actuality the deeds of the children reveal what lay in the depths of the father's heart, wherefore children are termed toledot.

column11: Eruvin 21b: ‘With regard to the verse, “His head is as the most fine gold, his locks [kevutzotav] are wavy [taltalim], and black as a raven” (Song of Songs 5:11), Rav Ḥisda said that Mar Ukva said: This teaches that it is possible to expound from each and every stroke [kotz] of the letters in the Torah mounds upon mounds [tilei tilim] of laws.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Eruvin 21b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and on this they said (Eruvin 21b) on the verse "His locks are curled": that one may expound upon every single stroke heaps upon heaps of halachot. And it corresponds to the moon which similarly...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column12: Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1:20
column13: And according to this foundational approach, the entire Tractate of Eruvin and its teachings were established: to transform the public domain (Reshut HaRabim / the realm of apparent multiplicity and division) into the single, unified domain of the One (Reshut HaYachid). This enactiment was instituted by King Solomon, peace be upon him—the builder of the Holy Temple—who fashioned metaphorical handles/ears (oznayim) for the Torah (as stated in Eruvin 21b), meaning accessible handles to grasp, given that the commandments of the Torah are thoroughly embedded in physical action.
column15: What is the meaning of “His locks are curled (taltalim)”? Upon every stroke and serif (kotz) are mounds upon mounds (tilei tilim) of halakhot. How so? It is written in it: “Neither shall you profane,” etc.

column11: Bava Batra 4a: ‘Herod said to him: I am he. Had I known that the Sages were so cautious I would not have killed them. column11: Tikkunei Zohar 77b:4-78a:3: “In Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 36, 77b), the verse ‘Let there be light, and there was light’ is expounded on the two heads of the year: ‘Let there be light (Yehi Ohr)’ refers to Nisan and Passover, when the light of Chesed shines from Above; ‘and there was light (Vayehi Ohr)’ refers to Tishrei and Rosh Hashanah, when Israel awakens the light of Torah from below through judgment and repentance.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 77b:4-78a:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“And behold it is stated in the holy books that Chanukah is the final sealing from Rosh Hashanah, – and this alludes to the words of the Tikunim (Tikun 36): "'And there was light' — this is Rosh...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is the meaning of "so that an impure spirit should rest upon him"— for whatever is the antithesis of holiness is impurity. In contrast, boundary against envy is mediated through natural desire, and even when not for Heaven's sake, it produces good; as written in holy books that charity given not for its own sake is still good, since it nevertheless sustains the poor man, and contributes to the welfare of the world.
column15: The second, “and there was light,” denotes tangible existence, corresponding to gestation/conception, and to Noah: for with Noah Hashem established an enduring covenant demonstrating that life would permanently persist.

column11: Tikkunei Zohar 77b:4-78a:3: “In Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 36, 77b), the verse ‘Let there be light, and there was light’ is expounded on the two heads of the year: ‘Let there be light (Yehi Ohr)’ refers to Nisan and Passover, when the light of Chesed shines from Above; ‘and there was light (Vayehi Ohr)’ refers to Tishrei and Rosh Hashanah, when Israel awakens the light of Torah from below through judgment and repentance.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 77b:4-78a:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this alludes to the words of the Tikunim (Tikun 36): "'And there was light' — this is Rosh Hashanah", which we explained that on every Rosh Hashanah comes a renewal of the light of the Oral...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And our father Isaac, peace be upon him, who embodied this attribute of judgment, had his vision dimmed through Esau's accusations which momentarily found favor in his eyes, rendering him unable to judge by external sight; meriting instead the higher perception of the heart during the blessing, which is the perception of the Tetragrammaton—the rung of Jacob—illuminating before his eyes; matching the declaration: "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which Hashem has blessed," using the Tetragrammaton, having smelled the fragrance of his future betrayers who are nonetheless full of holiness.
column15: “The eye of a fine needle”—this denotes a minute aperture of pure radiance through which the cleft (sedek)—the concealing rift dividing the universe from God's light—could be bridged; through it they would perceive that there is no autonomous innovation in creation.

column11: Sotah 47b: ‘From the time when women with “stretched-forth necks and wanton eyes” (Isaiah 3:16) proliferated, the bitter waters of a sota proliferated, as more people were suspected of committing adultery; but they eventually ceased when licentiousness became too widespread. From the time when those who accept gifts proliferated, the days decreased and the years shortened, as it is written: “And he who hates gifts lives” (Proverbs 15:27). From the time when those with boastful [zeḥuḥei] hearts proliferated, dispute proliferated in Israel. From the time when the students of Shammai and Hillel who did not serve their Rabbis sufficiently proliferated, dispute proliferated in Israel, and the Torah…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 47b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And behold in Rashi's commentary (Sotah 47b) he explained: – "A man who has everything in him" — Torah in its absolute truth without flaw, forgetfulness, or dispute, and that matches what is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And nevertheless it is likewise true that accepting gifts shortens life, as stated in Sotah (47b): "When those who accept gifts multiplied, days were diminished and years were shortened"; and the meaning of this dual phrasing is: human life is allotted in a number of years; wherefore Kiddushin (38a) states: "Hashem completes the years of the righteous from day to day"; completing his decreed years, whereas if one lacks merit, they do not complete a full year.
column15: And this is: “Tohu is something that confounds people” — meaning that creatures can be misled into drawing haughty self-assurance from it. And this is: “Bohu — it is in it” (bo hu), as my revered father explained: that in this very realization that Hashem desires his service, from that very thing Hashem expects the Jew to serve Him with even deeper devotion.

column11: Rosh Hashanah 18a: ‘With regard to this verse Rava said: With sacrifice or offering the sin of Eli’s house is not atoned, but it can be atoned through Torah study. Abaye said: With sacrifice or offering the sin of Eli’s house is not atoned, but it is atoned through Torah study and the performance of acts of kindness. It is related that Rabba and Abaye came from the house of Eli, which was subject to the curse that most of its members would die young. Rabba, who engaged almost exclusively in Torah study, lived for forty years, whereas Abaye, who engaged in both Torah study and in the performance of acts of kindness lived for sixty years.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Rosh Hashanah 18a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written (Rosh Hashanah 18a): "Abaye who engaged in Torah and lovingkindness"? And Torah without fear of Heaven the Gemara called (Yoma 72b) "a price in the hand of a fool" and it is not...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: These two Talmudic formulations correspond to the two spiritual rungs mentioned above. And the phrase "whoever engages in Torah and lovingkindness" implies the integration of all three pillars, omitting explicit mention of the pillar of Service (Avodah), in the manner of the verse: "By lovingkindness and truth iniquity is expiated" (Proverbs 16:6), where "truth" is Torah and "lovingkindness" is charity (Berakhot 5b), omitting sacrificial service; and in Sotah (44a) mentioning merely "Torah and good deeds," and in Rosh Hashanah (18a) regarding the House of Eli: "it shall not be expiated with sacrifice, but with Torah and lovingkindness," see there.
column15: So it was prior to creation, when the Torah preceded the world by two thousand supernal years, enfolded in divine Thought, subsequently cascading downward to human sight clothed in distinct hues and garments.

column11: Yoma 72b: ‘Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said that Rabbi Yonatan said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, as he has no heart?” (Proverbs 17:16)? This expresses the following sentiment: Woe to them, haters of Torah scholars, a euphemism for the Torah scholars themselves, who immerse themselves in Torah and have no fear of Heaven. They are fools; they try to acquire the wisdom of Torah, but since they have no fear of Heaven in their hearts they lack the ability to do so.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 72b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And Torah without fear of Heaven the Gemara called (Yoma 72b) "a price in the hand of a fool" and it is not considered Torah at all, and the Torah is called merely "the gate to the courtyard"...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: The primary seat of wisdom being in the brain, while in the heart resides desire. And lower wisdom is rooted in the heart's holy yearning, meaning a heart containing the fear of Heaven, the hallmark of the Jewish heart; but when devoid of fear of Heaven, concerning this it is said: "Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he has no heart to it?" (Mishlei 17:16); and the Sages in Yoma (72b) expounded this regarding those who study Torah without fear of Heaven in Israel.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 32:3
column15: “Bread” is merely the sustaining of the heart, that man perceive that the world and its fullness belong entirely to Hashem, and creatures have no independent share in ruling the world, Hashem alone directing it according to His gracious will; and accordingly man need not fear his fellow, and even the orphan who is among the vulnerable need not fear any creature, since he has upon Whom to lean and trust, in Him to Whom all dominion belongs, Who governs and guides the universe.

column11: Shabbat 88b: ‘And that is what Rava said: To those who are right-handed in their approach to Torah, and engage in its study with strength, good will, and sanctity, Torah is a drug of life, and to those who are left-handed in their approach to Torah, it is a drug of death. Alternatively, why are matters of Torah referred to as royal? Because to each and every utterance that emerged from the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, two crowns are tied. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “My beloved is to me like a bundle of myrrh that lies between my breasts” (Song of Songs 1:13)? And one...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is the serpentine skin, concerning which it is written (Yoma 72b): "If he merits not, it becomes for him an elixir of death"; and in Shabbat (88b): "to those who turn leftward it is a deadly poison", and: "transgressors shall fall therein". And our Sages expounded (Bamidbar Rabbah 14:22) that the Oral Torah was not committed to writing because the nations would otherwise translate it and claim "We are Israel"—meaning that with the external garment they share an affinity, it being the skin of the serpent.
column15: That is to say: precisely because Hashem set before man such dense garments, to the extent that it can seem to him that he can act against His will, and yet man, through his divine service, pierces through every kind of concealing garment — this is the ultimate triumph, and this is what is termed “turning oneself consciously toward the good.”

column11: Berakhot 11a: ‘The Gemara answers: It was necessary for him to add this reason, as if you say: Beit Hillel also hold that one is permitted to recite Shema while reclining and Rabbi Yishmael could have remained reclining even in accordance with the opinion of Beit Hillel, but this only applies when one had already been reclining originally, in which case it is like any other position. column13: So when one lacks companionship, he should immerse himself in Torah, for it is the blueprint of Creation and of all created beings, as they said in Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 1), and it turns out that he has the companionship of all Creation and the entire world. For this reason this world is called 'when you walk,' since walking signifies preoccupation, as they stated in Berakhot (11a): 'When you walk, etc.' – this refers to preoccupation with a mitzvah.
column15: And the meaning is as we explained: if man looks not upon the outer garment of these gifts but at what he derives from their inwardness—namely Heavenly glory—they are truly good gifts, but not otherwise.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 9: ‘In Rabbi Meir’s Torah they found written: “And, behold, it was very [me’od] good” – and, behold, death [mot] is good. Rabbi Meir had written mot. Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥman said: I was once riding on the shoulders of my grandfather, going up from his city to Kefar Ḥanan via Beit She’an, and I heard Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar sitting and expounding in the name of Rabbi Meir: “And, behold, it was very good” – and, behold, death is good. Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina and Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina said: Adam the first man was worthy not to have tasted the taste of death. Why, then, was he penalized with mortality? column13: Concerning this the Sages taught (Kiddushin 30b): "I created the Evil Inclination, and I created the Torah as its seasoning spice." Literally like a culinary spice that seasons the food until that dish becomes "very good," matching Bereishit Rabbah (9:7) on: "'And behold, it was very good' (Genesis 1:31)—this is the Evil Inclination."
column15: This is because the primary love of the Blessed Name resides in the very inception of a thing and in its primordial seed, while all the rest is unfolding commentary; and from that first point everything branches forth and spreads.

column11: Shabbat 149b: ‘Having quoted Rabbi Ya’akov, son of the daughter of Ya’akov, the Gemara brings another teaching of this amora. column13: That is, because the Blessed Name does not desire that there exist in the world a creature who causes harm to another creature. And thus acted that pious man in Ta'anit 24a Rabbi Yosi of Yukrat who prayed that his daughter return to her dust so that men would not stumble into sin because of her; and so pleaded that maiden in Sotah 22a that men should not stumble through her beauty, as written in Shabbat 149b: "Anyone on whose account his fellow is punished, etc."

column15: “Unto the land that I will show you”—corresponds to the War of the Kings, where superficially it appeared as a fault that he slew those souls; for to chastise a person with afflictions is legitimate retribution for his wicked deeds, yet to slay a human soul implies accusing the Artisan Who fashioned this soul with inherent deficiency, asserting he has no right to live in the world because his soul was flawed from creation.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 4: ‘“God made the firmament, and divided between the water that was under the firmament and the water that was above the firmament; and it was so” (Genesis 1:7). “God made the firmament” – this is one of the verses due to which ben Zoma stirred up commotion in the world. “[God] made”? This is bewildering; for were they not [brought about] by God’s mere word? That is, “By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; by the breath of His mouth, all their hosts” (Psalms 33:6). Why is “that it was good” not written regarding the second day? column13: And regarding Joseph—his facial countenance mirrored his father Jacob (Bereishis Rabbah 84:8); for "the beauty of Jacob mirrored the beauty of Adam HaRishon," as stated in Bava Metzia (84a); implying that from Adam until Jacob no such radiant beauty existed; and in the Torah physical beauty in a man is recorded in Joseph: "And Joseph was of beautiful form, and fair to look upon" (Bereishis 39:6); which was an extraordinary spiritual beauty, reflecting the beauty of Jacob.
column15: This parallels the halakhic principle regarding forbidden items of benefit (issurei hana'ah), which are disqualified from mitzvot requiring a physical measure because “their measure is considered crushed to powder” (kittutei mikatat shiureih), yet valid for mitzvot requiring no measure.

column11: Berakhot 55a: ‘On a similar note, Rabbi Yoḥanan said: The Holy One, Blessed be He, only grants wisdom to one who already possesses wisdom, as it is stated: “He gives wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to they who know understanding” (Daniel 2:21). column13: The essence of wisdom and knowledge exists only when absorbed deeply into the heart, as stated concerning Doeg in Sanhedrin [106b] that his Torah was merely from the lips outward and not internalized, and "the Merciful One desires the heart," requiring that knowledge be absorbed within and that the heart be guided by that wisdom; which is termed "wise of heart," as Scripture states: "And into the heart of all who are wise-hearted I have put wisdom," derived in Berakhot [55a] that He grants wisdom only to the wise.
column15: “By His knowledge the depths were broken open”—notice it does not say generically “with knowledge” (be-da'at) as it says “with wisdom” and “with understanding,” but specifically “by His knowledge” (be-da'ato).

column13: And when she seeks to draw from lower wisdom which is the wisdom of women, and to gaze thereby through the window of intellect, she will be drawn through this toward the alien wisdom of the nations, whose entire wisdom is merely looking through the window, for among them there is no holy heart at all. Therefore Michal donned tefillin, which binds the Da'at of Israel unto Hashem, blessed be He, meaning that Chokhmah and Binah are bound through Da'at which connects them directly to Hashem, blessed be He.
column15: If one merits one of them he gains the treasure of the whole world: meriting wisdom he merits all, meriting strength he merits all, meriting wealth he merits all; when? When they are received as gifts from Heaven.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 65: ‘“Jacob approached Isaac his father and he felt him, and he said: The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Genesis 27:22). “Jacob approached Isaac…The voice is the voice of Jacob” – this voice is the voice of a wise man, but his hands are those that flay dead animals. Another matter, “the voice is the voice of Jacob” – Jacob rules only with his voice. “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” – Esau rules only with his hands. Another matter, “the voice is the voice of Jacob” – Rabbi Pinḥas said: The voice of Jacob withdraws into itself. suggests that the fact that the word hakol is without a vav it can be read as if the voice of…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 65) to illuminate his exposition here (“when the Sages sensed then at the close of the years of Yose ben Yoezer who was martyred during the Greek decrees (Bereishit Rabbah 65) that "the heart had diminished" as stated in the Gemara,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For it was then clarified that all was absolute truth: he was the true firstborn by divine intent and through purchase from Esau. And in donning Esau's garments, Jacob's holy action involved an external clothing associated with Esau, which for Esau were garments donned when attending his father (Bereishit Rabbah 65) to deceive him like a swine displaying its split hooves to appear kosher; and through those garments donned by Jacob, Isaac smelled the scent of Israel's future renegades (Sanhedrin 37a).
column15: Yet they approached from another angle, saying: since nature was empowered to proceed according to its ordinary routine during the era when Hashem conducts reality with forbearance and patience toward man.

column11: Chagigah 3b: ‘Lest a person say: Now, how can I study Torah when it contains so many different opinions? The verse states that they are all “given from one shepherd.” One God gave them; one leader, i.e., Moses, said them from the mouth of the Master of all creation, Blessed be He, as it is written: “And God spoke all these words” (Exodus 20:1). The plural form “words” indicates that God transmitted all the interpretations of the Ten Commandments. Since the Sages invariably utilize the Torah itself or the statements of the prophets as the sources for their opinions, there is a certain unity to the study of Torah, despite the numerous explanations and applications.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 5, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 3b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And this is the meaning of what Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said (Chagigah 3b) on the verse "The words of the wise, etc., masters of assemblies": "These declare impure and these declare pure, etc.,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For behold (Chagigah 3b): it is a Halachah given to Moses at Sinai that Ammon and Moab separate the poor man's tithe during the Sabbatical year so that the poor of Israel may rely upon them, even though the Torah states explicitly: "Then I will command My blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years" (Leviticus 25:21).
column15: And this was Rabbi Yitzchak’s challenge—not merely on the literary opening of the Torah, but upon the ontological creation of light itself: that reality should have commenced only from the Exodus era.

column11: Chullin 92a: ‘Similar to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba’s interpretation of the word vine as an allusion to the Jewish people, Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says: This nation is likened to a vine. The branches of the vine support the clusters of grapes, the leaves, and the tendrils; these are represented among the Jewish people by the homeowners, who provide financial support for the entire nation.
